channel.title: No_code on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in No_code on Best of AI

item.title: Baserow
item.description:
Baserow gives teams an easy way to build databases. It looks like a spreadsheet, but tables can link to each other, store different field types, and show data as a grid, gallery, kanban board, calendar, or form. People without coding skills build trackers, inventories, and small internal tools with it.

It is open source, so companies can run it on their own servers, which appeals to those with data residency or privacy needs. The platform has a REST API and webhooks, an application builder for interfaces, and automations that run on triggers. An AI assistant can create tables from a prompt, and AI fields can generate or classify values for each row.

item.title: Microsoft Power Apps
item.description:
Power Apps lets people without a programming background build apps for their organization. Makers choose canvas apps, where you design screens by dragging controls, or model-driven apps that are generated from a data model. Typical uses include inspection forms, approval workflows, inventory trackers, and internal portals that replace spreadsheets and email chains. Apps run on web and mobile and integrate with Microsoft 365 and Teams.

It connects to a large range of data through connectors, including SharePoint, SQL Server, Salesforce, and Dataverse, Microsoft’s data platform. Power Automate adds workflow logic, and Power BI provides reporting. Copilot can create an app or a table from a plain-language description and help with formulas, and newer features allow building apps by chatting with an agent. Governance tools let IT manage environments and data policies.

item.title: NocoDB
item.description:
NocoDB turns a database into something that feels like Airtable. Connect it to an existing SQL database or create a new one, and users see tables as spreadsheets they can filter, sort, and edit, with views as kanban boards, galleries, calendars, and forms. Non-technical colleagues get access to data without learning SQL.

It generates REST and GraphQL APIs for tables, supports permissions and webhooks, and offers automation and an AI assistant to help with fields and queries. Because it is open source, teams can host it themselves and keep data on their own servers.

item.title: Squarespace
item.description:
Squarespace appeals to people who want an attractive site without a developer. You choose a template, change the content with a visual editor, and publish with hosting, security, and a domain included. Its designs are known for clean layouts and good typography, which makes it popular with creatives, small businesses, restaurants, and portfolio sites.

The platform goes beyond static pages. Built-in commerce handles products, subscriptions, and checkout, email campaigns support marketing, and Acuity Scheduling covers appointments. AI features include a site builder that generates a starting design and content from answers to a few questions, text-writing assistance, and tools for improving search visibility. Analytics show traffic and sales.

item.title: Thunkable
item.description:
Thunkable lets people build mobile apps without writing code. The designer places buttons, lists, maps, and other components on a screen, and a visual blocks editor, similar to Scratch, defines the logic. A live test app on your phone shows changes as you make them, which makes learning fast.

Apps are native, not just web wrappers, and can use device features like the camera, location, and notifications. Connections to databases, APIs, and services like Firebase and Airtable allow real functionality. Schools use Thunkable to teach app creation, and small businesses and entrepreneurs use it to build prototypes and simple tools.

item.title: WordPress
item.description:
WordPress is the software behind a large share of the web. You install it on a web host or sign up with a hosted service, and manage pages, posts, media, and users from a dashboard. A block editor lets you build layouts visually, and thousands of themes control how a site looks. Plugins extend it for SEO, contact forms, memberships, caching, analytics, and online stores through WooCommerce.

It comes in two forms that are easy to confuse. WordPress.org is the free software you host yourself, which gives full control and requires handling hosting, updates, and security. WordPress.com is a hosted service from Automattic with plans that handle those chores. AI arrives mostly through add-ons: Jetpack and other plugins offer writing help, image generation, and chat assistants, and AI site builders can generate a first draft of a site from a prompt. The core project is also adding building blocks for AI features.

item.title: DhiWise
item.description:
DhiWise sits between design and development. A designer prepares screens in Figma, and DhiWise generates app code, including navigation, state management, and connections to APIs defined by a specification. The output follows common project structure, so developers can continue in their own tools.

It speaks to teams that build many similar screens and want consistency. Developers use it to produce the first version of the user interface and wiring, then refine business logic by hand. AI features add the ability to generate code from prompts and to adapt designs.

item.title: Hocoos
item.description:
Hocoos aims at people who want a website without a design process. The user answers questions about their business and style, and the AI generates pages, text, and images, and sets up features such as contact forms, an online store, or appointment booking. An editor allows changes afterward.

The platform includes hosting, a domain option, and SEO basics, plus marketing helpers such as email tools and social media content. It is positioned for small and local businesses and solo entrepreneurs who need an online presence quickly.

item.title: 10Web
item.description:
10Web combines site generation with hosting. You describe a business or enter the address of an existing website, and the AI builds a WordPress site with layout, text, and images, which you can then edit with a visual builder based on Elementor. The result is a standard WordPress site, so it can use the plugin and theme ecosystem and can be moved elsewhere.

Hosting and optimization are part of the package. Sites run on managed WordPress hosting with a focus on speed, including automatic optimization of images and code to improve page speed scores, and tools for backups and security. AI features generate copy, images, and SEO suggestions, and an assistant can edit pages based on instructions. Agencies can white-label the platform and manage client sites, and there is an API for builders who want to embed it.

item.title: Adalo
item.description:
Adalo lets people without programming skills build mobile apps. You design screens with a drag-and-drop editor, add components such as lists, forms, and buttons, set up a database for your data, and define what happens when users interact. It handles user accounts, payments, and push notifications, and produces apps that can be published to the Apple App Store and Google Play, as well as web apps.

AI features speed up the first draft: you can describe an app and have the builder generate screens and data structures, then refine them manually. A marketplace of components and integrations extends functionality, and connections to external databases and APIs allow more complex apps. Typical projects include community directories, booking apps, marketplaces, internal tools, and simple social apps.

item.title: Airtable
item.description: Airtable looks like a spreadsheet but behaves like a database. Records live in tables with typed fields such as dates, attachments, checkboxes, and links to records in other tables, which allows relationships that spreadsheets cannot handle. The same data can be shown as a grid, kanban board, calendar, gallery, or timeline, and filters and groups tailor each view. It’s used for content calendars, product roadmaps, CRM, event planning, and operations.

item.title: AppSheet
item.description:
AppSheet lets people create business apps without programming. You point it at data in Google Sheets, Excel, a database, or another source, and AppSheet generates an app with views, forms, and actions. Typical uses include field service, inspections, inventory tracking, approvals, and data collection, where workers need to capture information on a phone, with photos, barcodes, GPS, and signatures.

AI helps create apps. Gemini can build an app from a plain-language description, and an assistant can suggest improvements and write expressions. Automation features, called bots, trigger actions such as sending emails, updating records, or creating documents when data changes, and integrations connect with Google Workspace, Apps Script, and other services. Governance features cover access control and deployment for organizations.

item.title: Bubble
item.description:
Bubble lets people build real web apps without programming. The editor works by placing elements on a page, defining a database, and setting up workflows that say what happens when a user clicks or a condition occurs. Apps can include logins, payments, and integrations with other services.

It is used for marketplaces, internal tools, SaaS products, and prototypes, and some companies run substantial businesses on it. AI features can generate a starting app or page layout from a description, and plugins extend functionality. Bubble hosts the app, so there is no server to manage.

item.title: Bubble
item.description: Bubble lets people build real software without writing code. You design pages by dragging elements onto a canvas, define what happens when users click or submit with visual workflows, and store data in a built-in database. That is enough to build marketplaces, internal tools, customer portals, and SaaS products. Because the logic is visual but still detailed, Bubble apps can be quite complex, which is why it has been popular with founders who want to test an idea before hiring developers.

item.title: Durable
item.description:
Durable promises a website with minimal effort. You tell it the kind of business you run and where you are, and it builds a site with pages, copy, images, and a layout in under a minute, which you can then edit with simple controls. It’s aimed at freelancers and local service businesses, such as plumbers, photographers, and consultants, who need an online presence quickly.

Beyond the site, Durable includes small-business tools. A built-in CRM tracks leads and customers, an invoicing feature handles billing, and AI assistants help write blog posts, social content, and marketing copy. It offers hosting and a custom domain, and basic analytics. Everything lives in one account, so owners avoid piecing together several services.

item.title: FlutterFlow
item.description: FlutterFlow combines the speed of a visual builder with real code. You design screens by dragging widgets, define logic with a visual action editor, and connect to backends such as Firebase, Supabase, or any API. Because it generates Flutter code, apps run natively on iOS and Android and also on the web, and you can export the code to continue development in a standard IDE, which avoids the lock-in of many no-code tools.

item.title: Framer
item.description:
Framer started as a prototyping tool and became a full website builder. Designers lay out pages on a canvas much like they do in Figma, set up responsive behavior, add animations and interactions, and publish to a fast hosted site with a custom domain. Because it gives designers precise control over visuals and motion, it’s popular for portfolios, landing pages, and marketing sites.

A CMS manages blog posts and other structured content, and features for SEO, localization, and analytics support production sites. AI tools generate a first draft of a site from a description, create wireframes, and write copy, which speeds up the start of a project. Components and code overrides allow customization when needed, and a marketplace of templates and plugins helps.

item.title: Glide
item.description:
Glide lets people build working apps from a spreadsheet. You connect a sheet or a table, and Glide generates an interface with lists, detail pages, forms, and actions, which you can customize with a visual editor. Because the data lives in a familiar place, small business owners and operations teams can create apps for inventory, field reports, event check-ins, and customer portals without writing code.

The platform has added more advanced features over time. Users can set up roles and permissions, run workflows that send emails or update records, and connect to services through integrations. AI features can generate apps from a description, extract data from images and documents, and add AI-powered actions such as summarizing or categorizing. Glide’s own database supports larger datasets than a typical spreadsheet.

item.title: Plasmic
item.description:
Plasmic connects visual design with real code. Developers register their React components in Plasmic, and designers and marketers can then drag those components onto a canvas, adjust styling and content, and publish pages without waiting for a code release. Alternatively, Plasmic can build entire pages and sites itself, and its output integrates with frameworks like Next.js, Gatsby, and plain React.

Features help teams collaborate. A CMS stores content, responsive design controls handle layouts across devices, and the editor includes interactions, animations, and data bindings. Teams can use it to build landing pages, marketing sites, and web apps, while developers stay in control of the underlying components. Code can be exported or used with a runtime, which reduces lock-in.

item.title: Retool AI
item.description:
Retool is designed for engineers who need to build internal software quickly. Developers connect databases, APIs, and services, drag components such as tables, forms, and charts onto a canvas, and write queries and logic in SQL and JavaScript where needed. The result is an application for operations, support, or finance teams to manage data, approve requests, or run workflows, built in hours instead of weeks.

AI is integrated across the platform. A generative assistant can create an app from a description, write queries, and generate components, and Retool offers AI actions to classify, summarize, and extract information as parts of apps and workflows. Retool Agents let teams build agents that use their data and tools, and workflows automate scheduled and event-driven tasks. Enterprise controls cover permissions, audit logs, and self-hosting.

item.title: Softr
item.description:
Softr turns data into software. A user connects Airtable, Google Sheets, or its own database, and builds pages with blocks such as lists, forms, dashboards, and charts. Logins and permissions control which users see which records.

Typical products include client portals, directories, simple CRMs, and internal tools. The AI builder creates an app from a description, and workflows automate actions. Hosting and a custom domain are included.

Softr has a free plan and paid tiers by users and features. Complex logic is limited compared with full code. Alternatives include Glide, Pory, Stacker, Bubble, and Retool. Softr suits non-developers building apps on spreadsheets and databases.

item.title: Webflow
item.description:
Webflow sits between simple site builders and hand-coded sites. Designers work on a canvas that mirrors how the web works, setting classes, flexbox and grid layouts, and breakpoints, and the platform produces production code and hosts the result. That gives far more control than template-based builders, which is why agencies and in-house design teams like it.

The platform includes a CMS for blogs and collections, e-commerce, interactions and animations, localization, and tools for marketers to edit content without breaking the design. AI features generate sections and copy, suggest changes, and help with site structure and SEO. Developers can add custom code and use an API to connect Webflow to other services.

item.title: Wix ADI
item.description:
Wix ADI, short for Artificial Design Intelligence, was an early attempt at automatic site building. A user answered questions about their business and style, and ADI generated a layout with text, images, and a structure suited to the industry. It let people with no design skills get a website online in minutes, long before generative AI was common.

ADI sites had limits. They used a simpler editor than the main Wix Editor, which made it hard to customize them or to add advanced features. Wix has since retired the product: ADI sites are no longer supported and existing ones were moved into the standard Wix Editor, so owners can keep editing them there.

item.title: Zapier
item.description:
Zapier lets people automate work between apps without programming. A Zap starts with a trigger, such as a new form entry, and performs actions in other apps, like adding a row to a spreadsheet and sending a Slack message. It connects thousands of products.

AI has become part of the platform. Users describe an automation in plain language, add AI steps that summarize or classify data, and build agents that act across apps. Tables, forms, and interfaces let teams build small apps around their automations.

item.title: Pory
item.description:
Pory turns spreadsheets and databases into websites. A user connects an Airtable base or Google Sheet, designs pages and layouts with a visual editor, and publishes a directory, portal, or dashboard. Logins and permissions control who sees what.

It is popular for member directories, job boards, simple CRMs, and client portals. Because the data stays in the source, updating the spreadsheet updates the site.

Pory has a free tier and paid plans. Complex logic is limited compared with full app builders. Alternatives include Softr, Glide, Stacker, Noloco, and Bubble. Pory suits non-developers building front ends on Airtable or Sheets.

item.title: Base44
item.description:
Base44 lets someone describe an app in a chat and get a working version. The platform generates the interface, data model, logic, and authentication, hosts it, and lets the user keep refining by asking for changes. Because the backend is included, there is no need to wire up separate services.

It is popular for internal tools, simple customer portals, and prototypes. Users can add integrations, such as email and payments, and publish with a custom domain. The platform is part of Wix, which gives it a route to a large base of small business customers.

item.title: Dora
item.description:
Dora targets people who want a standout site without writing code. A user describes the site or starts from a template, and the platform generates pages with 3D objects, scroll animations, and interactions, which are expensive to build by hand. A visual editor lets them adjust layout, copy, and motion.

Designers and small businesses use it for portfolios, landing pages, and marketing sites where visual impact matters. Compared with simple builders, it emphasizes motion and depth. Published sites are hosted by the platform, and exporting options vary by plan.

item.title: Floot
item.description:
Floot belongs to the family of prompt-to-app builders. A user describes what they want, such as a booking tool or a simple marketplace, and the platform generates a working application with interface, logic, and data storage, hosts it, and lets the user keep refining by chat.

The target is non-technical founders who want to test an idea without hiring developers. Quick prototypes help validate demand and communicate a concept to partners or investors. Generated apps need testing and security review before handling real customers or payments.

item.title: InstaWebAI
item.description:
InstaWebAI generates a full website from a short brief. A user enters information about the business, and the tool creates pages, copy, images, and a structure designed for search engines, which can be edited and published. The goal is to cut the time from idea to live site to minutes.

It targets owners who lack design or writing skills and want a professional baseline. Typical outputs include home, services, about, and contact pages, along with metadata for search visibility. Publishing options and domain connections vary by plan.

item.title: Whacka
item.description:
Whacka belongs to the prompt-to-app builders. A user explains the product, and the platform generates screens, back-end logic, and data storage, previews it, and deploys it online. Changes happen through conversation.

It suits prototypes, internal tools, and tests of demand. Generated apps require testing, and security and data handling deserve review before real users or payments are involved.

Independent information is limited. Whacka has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Lovable, Bolt, Replit, Base44, and Rocket. Whacka suits non-technical founders prototyping.
